rule: Design for a strong, iconic silhouette first; details embellish the design but do not determine it.
A design should be understandable within three seconds.
Squint to see only major shapes and values; if those read correctly the design works.
View the work at postage-stamp size to expose composition, design and value errors hidden by detail.
Flip the image horizontally or view it in a mirror to spot perspective and proportion errors.
Small alterations to familiar forms create convincing designs; restraint is often the secret.
Keep a creature readable by giving it a recognisable head; that gives it personality.
Darker shadow tones push lighter shapes forward; add darks where shapes read confusingly.
Negative shapes around a form create its silhouette and are as important as the positive shapes.
Keep edges sharpest at the focal point and softer elsewhere; vary edge quality.
Define details in order of visual interest, usually starting at the head.
Line quality suggests material: quick hard strokes for hard surfaces, gentle slower strokes for soft organic forms.
Keeping the nearest part lighter while darkening the rest pulls the eye forward and adds dimension.
